Triggers.value: People who look similar to the victims

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I detach myself from the memories

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: The inaction/self-blame item is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. In a child victim context, 'not doing more to stop what happened' implies agency that is typically not clinically plausible for the same trauma profile; a more general shame/self-blame item would fit, but this specific omission-guilt wording is questionable.

Within the Threat node, 'difficulty concentrating' is not a threat appraisal but a general arousal/cognitive symptom. The other Threat items reflect current danger and hypervigilance ('strong physical reactions to reminders', 'need to stay alert to fall asleep'). This item weakens within-node coherence and does not match the node's formulation role as perceived current threat.

vignette:
Keoni had been six years old the first time his father's lighter clicked near his skin. The flame never touched him directly-his father was too clever for that-but the stench of singed cotton and melting nylon from his own shirt had seared itself into his memory. That smell meant he had done something wrong again, meant his father's hand would follow the flame, meant he would be held down until he stopped crying. By the time Keoni turned nine, he had learned to keep his face flat and his voice low, because any flicker of happiness was a provocation. A smile meant he was getting too comfortable, and comfort was a crime. So he buried every good feeling before it could show, and the habit never left him.

Now, at fifty-six, Keoni worked as a detective in a medium-sized city. The job had seemed like a natural fit when he was younger-he was watchful, could read a room without being read, and had a memory for details others missed. But the same vigilance that made him good at his work had turned into a constant, grinding hyperarousal. He could not sit with his back to a door. He could not sleep through the night because his body insisted on staying alert, listening for footsteps that never came. When a child-victim case crossed his desk, he would study the photographs with a clenched jaw, seeing not a stranger's face but his own small, terrified reflection. He would push the file away and mutter about needing coffee, but the rage was already building-a hot, wordless fury that left him shaking and unable to focus on the next page. That rage was the only emotion that ever felt clean. Positive emotions, the rare moments of genuine warmth or contentment, filled him with an unnamed dread, as if they were a trap waiting to snap shut.

The abuse had shattered something deeper than trust. As a child, Keoni had believed the world made sense-that adults protected children, that home was safe, that if you followed the rules you would be okay. His father's hand had taken all of that apart, piece by piece. By the time he was twelve, he had come to see the world as a place where danger lurked in every smile, where kindness was a mask for cruelty, and where no amount of caution could ever guarantee safety. That belief never left him. He had carried it into his marriage, his work, every relationship. He had come to believe that the abuse had happened because of who he was-he was a lousy coper, he told himself, look at how he still flinched at a burnt match, how his hands would tremble when he passed a man wearing a certain style of work shirt. He had stopped wearing button-downs himself, and he avoided the grocery store after five o'clock because too many fathers came in straight from construction jobs, their clothes smelling of sweat and smoke. He had also learned to detach from the memories when they surfaced, to step outside his own mind and watch the scene from a distance. The problem was that they often surfaced without warning-a whiff of something acrid on the street, and suddenly he was back in the kitchen, pinned on the linoleum, the lighter clicking again. He could never explain what had happened in those moments; when he tried to tell a colleague or even his ex-wife, his thoughts would dissolve into a tangle of fragments, and he would trail off mid-sentence, unable to finish.

The divorce had been quiet and final. His wife had said he was never really there, that he had stopped letting her in years ago. She was right. Avoidance had become his default. He kept his social circle small, then nonexistent. He worked late into the night, alone in his office, because there were fewer people to watch. The hypervigilance never rested, but at least when he was alone, no one could notice the way he scanned every corner of a room. Even now, he was certain that the world was fundamentally dangerous-that no one could really be trusted, that safety was a lie people told themselves. That was why he never let anyone close. That was why, when a colleague offered help, he saw a threat.

What finally brought Keoni to the clinic was a case three weeks earlier. He had been called to a house fire that had killed a child. The smell of burnt insulation and melted plastics had hit him before he even stepped out of the car. He had frozen on the sidewalk, his heart hammering, his vision tunneling. For a long minute he had not known where or when he was. A younger officer had touched his elbow, asking if he was okay, and Keoni had snapped at him, then retreated to his car and driven home without a word. The next morning, his captain told him he was taking mandatory leave and gave him a list of therapists approved for department referrals. Keoni had taken the list because refusing would have raised more questions, but he still was not sure he could sit in a room and tell a stranger the whole story-especially because he was certain that once he started, he would not be able to explain it clearly, and the stranger would see exactly what kind of person he really was. And even if he did explain, he doubted anything could change his belief that the world was simply not safe, and never would be.
